profile.summary: Micah presents an announcement of God's judgment against false prophets, unfaithful leaders and rich oppressors, but does not contain the divine word in the ruin: after the punishment, come restoration. The book shows that the Lord will expose the sin of Israel and Judah, permit devastation as a consequence of infidelity, and yet will preserve a remnant, renew his people and fulfill his promises. At the center of hope is the promise of a ruler coming from Bethlehem, through whom God would subdue enemies and lead his people to a future of peace and fidelity.
profile.setting: Micah prophesied in the period of the kings of Judah Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, when both Israel and Judah lived in strong moral and religious corruption, with social oppression, economic injustice, political intrigue, deception and violence. The historical setting includes the decay of true worship, the Assyrian pressure on the region, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and the threat to Jerusalem during the reign of Hezekiah. The authorship is attributed to Morésete's prophet Micah, but the introduction recognizes that some see the possibility of later editing in final form, without this being necessary to understand the book.

structure.label: Superscription and opening of the confrontation
structure.description: Introduces the prophet and presents the tone of divine warning against the sin of Israel and Judah.

structure.label: First call to listen
structure.description: First major section of denunciation and judgment, focusing on the sin of the people and the consequences of infidelity.

structure.label: Second call to listen
structure.description: Condemn leaders, oppressors, false prophets, and religious and social corruption.

structure.label: Hope for the last days
structure.description: Interscale judgment with a promise of restoration, gathering the people and pointing to God's future.

structure.label: The ruler of Bethlehem and the victory of the Lord
structure.description: It highlights the promise of the ruler who will come from Bethlehem and the subjugation of the enemies of the people of God.

structure.label: Third call to listen
structure.description: Retake the Lord's accusation against the people, showing the gravity of their unfaithfulness and wrongedness.

structure.label: Least, pardon and restoration
structure.description: It concludes with the tension between the deserved ruin and hope in forgiveness, compassion and final restoration.

themes: God's judgment against infidelity and oppression
The remnant as God's renewed people
The Promise of the Ruler from Bethlehem
God's faithfulness to the promises made to Abraham and Jacob
readingKeys: Notice how the book alternates severe denunciations and promises of hope; restoration does not deny judgment, but comes through it.
Note the targeted groups: false prophets, corrupt leaders, rich oppressors, and the whole nation, showing that sin is both public and structural.
Realize the recurrence of the call to "ouvir," which organizes the book in large blocks and highlights the authority of the word of God.
profile.cautions: The introduction indicates that the exact date and the final form of the book are discussed: there is a later editing proposal, but this is not necessary to accept the main message. It is also necessary to read the prophetic images as figurative language, used to describe real events and the announcement of judgment and hope, without forcing chronological details beyond what the source allows.

dossier.narratedEra: The book is set in the 8th century BC, during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in Judah, with the political scene of Israel and Judah under Assyrian pressure, before the fall of Samaria (722 BC) and with the horizon also turned to the later threat over Jerusalem.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes present the prophecy as a message originally given by Micah in the pre-exile period, with the possibility of final editing later at the beginning of the post-exile (538-458 BC). The sources also insist that the date of composition should not be confused with the historical setting of the prophecies; part of the material may reflect events of 722 BC and 701 BC, while some passages are seen by some as open to a post-exile framing, without this being necessary according to the source itself.

politics.title: Kingdoms of Judah and Israel under divided monarchy
politics.detail: Micah prophesies during the reigns of the kings of King Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The notes treat Samaria as the capital of the northern kingdom and Jerusalem as the capital of the south, sometimes functioning as the names of the nations themselves.
politics.readingImpact: Reading the book in this environment shows that judgment is not abstract: it reaches centers of power, leadership and national identity in both realms.

politics.title: Tension between Judah and Aman/Israel under Jothus
politics.detail: Jotham is described as relatively good king, but who did not remove the high places; therefore the Lord would have lifted up Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel to oppress Judah.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the book as a denunciation of sin even in periods of relative political stability; even the reign "better" still leaves room for divine discipline.

politics.title: Alliance of Ahaz with Assyria
politics.detail: Ahaz is portrayed as following forbidden practices and as an ally of Tiglate-Pileser III, by paying tribute with gold from the temple and the royal treasures. The notes link this to the corruption of the cult and the weakening of Judah before Assyria.
politics.readingImpact: Prophetic criticism gains clarity: the search for political security through pagan alliances appears as religious infidelity and erosion of allegiance to the Lord.

politics.title: Fall of Samaria and Northern exile
politics.detail: The notes claim that Samaria fell in 722 BC after siege of three years under Assyrian pressure, deporting the Israelites to provinces and vassal states of the empire.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that Micah's warnings against Samaria are not generic: they anticipate a concrete historical collapse that validates the weight of the announced judgment.

politics.title: Assyria as imperial force of devastation
politics.detail: The Assyrian march is associated with the advance of the coastal plain and the interior of Judah in 703-701 BC; the notes link to this the fall of several cities, including Laquis, in 701 BC, and the attack of Senaquerib.
politics.readingImpact: This background extends the reading of the laments and images of ruin in Micah 1, showing that the devastation language corresponds to a real military campaign.

politics.title: Jerusalem preserved, but Judah wounded
politics.detail: In 701 BC, Jerusalem was delivered from destruction by divine intervention, but Senaqueribe devastated about forty-six cities of Israel and Judah. The notes use this to show God's partial judgment and sovereignty over war.
politics.readingImpact: The preservation of Jerusalem is not a sign of national innocence; the city continues under moral judgment, even though it is spared from the total collapse.

customs.title: Worship in the Highs and Competition with the Temple
customs.detail: The notes mention the permanence of the "High"s in Judah under Jotham and then the introduction of pagan altars in Jerusalem by Ahaz, in contrast to the proper worship in the temple. They also point to syncretism and idolatry in Samaria and Jerusalem.
customs.readingImpact: The religious context makes the book a denunciation of the cult mixed: the problem is not only moral, but also liturgical and pactual loyalty.

customs.title: Child sacrifice, pagan incense and fertility
customs.detail: About Ahaz, the source mentions forbidden practices such as child sacrifice, burning pagan incense and fertility worship.
customs.readingImpact: These practices give concreteness to the prophetic accusations against religious corruption; the judgment of Micah is not a rhetorical exaggeration, but a response to serious perversions of the cult.

customs.title: The economic oppression of the rich
customs.detail: The introduction highlights the oppression of the poor by the rich, economic injustice and social violence as marks of Israel and Judah. In Micah 2 and 7, the oppressed appear in a framework of widespread exploitation.
customs.readingImpact: Reading the prophet with this background prevents the book from reducing the book to religious criticism only; fidelity to God includes just economy and lack of exploitation.

customs.title: Public mourning as a prophetic gesture
customs.detail: Micah is described as walking naked and barefoot in a sign of lament for the sentence against Samaria and Jerusalem. In 1:16, shaving the head is also presented as a sign of grief and despair, and possibly purification.
customs.readingImpact: The prophetic gesture intensifies the reading of the book: the words are accompanied by the corporal staging of judgment, inviting the reader to feel the weight of calamity.

customs.title: Community life eroded by fights and betrayal
customs.detail: In 7:1-6, the notes describe a society without law, justice or righteousness, where relatives and fellow citizens deceive each other, judges accept bribes, and social trust collapses.
customs.readingImpact: The final chapter is now read as a diagnosis of a disdainful community, not just individual sin; the promised restoration needs to rebuild broken relationships.

customs.title: Remanescent and return to territory
customs.detail: The notes speak of the rescue of a remnant, the return to land and the restoration of territories such as Bashan and Gilead, in addition to the language of recovered inheritance.
customs.readingImpact: Hope in Micah is not ethereal: it involves people, land, and restored belonging, which gives historical density to the promises of redemption.

language.title: The name Micahs and the chorus, "Who is like the Lord?"
language.detail: The notes note that Micah is probably a short form of Micaiah, with the sense "Who is like the Lord?" and relate this to the climax of 7:18-20.
language.readingImpact: The name of the prophet becomes a literary key to the closing of the book: the uniqueness of God is the theme that governs judgment and mercy.

language.title: "Ouvi" as called solemn
language.detail: In 1:2, "Attention!" translates the same word that introduces the Shema into Deuteronomy 6:4. The main sections of the book also begin with summons to listen.
language.readingImpact: This suggests that Micah speaks as a witness of alliance, not as a neutral observer; the reader should hear as one in front of a pactual appeal.

language.title: Image of theophany and cosmic sovereignty
language.detail: The mountains that melts, the Lord who the hills of the earth and the movement of creation are treated as the language of theophany. The notes oppose the Lord to Baal, emphasizing sovereignty over nations and nature.
language.readingImpact: Reading ceases to be only political and becomes cosmic: the judgment on Samaria and Judah is an expression of God's universal government.

language.title: Prostitution as a metaphor of infidelity
language.detail: In 1:6, prostitution is explained as a prophetic metaphor for God's abandonment in behalf of other gods, with a possible bond between idolatry and sexual practices in pagan cults.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands that sexual language is not decorative; it depicts rupture of alliance and deep religious corruption.

language.title: Sion exalted and pilgrimage of nations
language.detail: In 4:1-5, the notes highlight the elevation of the mountain of the house of the Lord, the teaching of the law to the nations, and the flow of peoples to worship. The image of "supposed in plowshares" is explained as a transformation of war instruments into production tools, although an alternative reading mentioned is the uselessness of the metal.
language.readingImpact: The text is read as an eschatological reversal of violence: war, insecurity and competition give way to learning, peace and prosperity.

language.title: Threshing floor, horns and hooves
language.detail: In 4:12-13, the image of the threshing and crushing is explained as a place of threshing and crushing, while horns, hooves, iron and bronze represent military strength. The term for "dedicator" is linked to the spoil that the Lord is dedicated.
language.readingImpact: The metaphor shows that the final victory belongs to the Lord, not to the empires; the same force that he judged Israel would also submit the nations.

language.title: The Remain and the Shepherd
language.detail: In 7:14, the image of the shepherd with staff is associated with protection against hostile nations; in 7:14-20, the text emphasizes loyal love (khesed), God's faithfulness and forgiveness.
language.readingImpact: Pastoral language reinforces that restoration is not only political, but relational and pactual; God acts as guardian and reconciling of the remnant.

timeline.title: Ministry of Micah in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah
timeline.detail: The notes place the prophetic activity over about 65 years of reigns, approximately between 750 and 686 BC, without stating that the whole book was pronounced at once.
timeline.readingImpact: The book should be read as a collection of messages over a long period, following real political and spiritual changes.

timeline.title: Before the fall of Samaria
timeline.detail: Some prophecies of Micah are presented as before 722 BC, especially those of judgment on Samaria.
timeline.readingImpact: This makes Micah a preventive voice: the prophet announces the disaster before it happens, and not later as mere historical commentary.

timeline.title: 722 BC: destruction of Samaria
timeline.detail: The fall of Samaria is treated as fulfillment of the judgment, with a three-year encircuming, capture of Hosea and dispersion of the Israelites between Assyrian provinces and vassal kingdoms.
timeline.readingImpact: Micah's warnings against the north acquire historical weight, and the reading of the book is now shaped by the reality of exile.

timeline.title: 701 BC: Assyrian campaign in Judah
timeline.detail: The Assyrian march is related to the events of 703-701 BC, with emphasis on the fall of Laquis in 701 BC and for the devastation of cities of Judah by Senaqueribe.
timeline.readingImpact: Micah 1 ceases to be only a generic threat and becomes theological reading of a specific military campaign that struck Judah deeply.

timeline.title: Two references to the prophecy: Jeremiah and Matthew
timeline.detail: The introduction of Matthew Henry notes that Micah 3:12 is quoted in Jeremiah 26:17-18, and that Micah 5:2 is quoted in Matthew 2:5-6. The notes use this to confirm the authority of the prophecy and its canonical reception.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader realizes that Micah's message continued to operate as a normative word and recognized long after its composition.

timeline.title: Return of exile in 538 BC and future restoration
timeline.detail: The notes of 7:11-12 include the beginning of the return of Babylonian exile in 538 BC and also an even greater final restoration; in 4:10-13, Babylon's language is treated as a symbol of exile and also as a later historical horizon.
timeline.readingImpact: Hope in Micah does not end in the collapse of Judah; the book projects return, discipline, and restoration into multiple temporal layers.

investigation: The source introduces a possible final post-exile edition, but states that this is not necessary to explain the book; this hypothesis remains only as a proposal of some interpreters.
There is strongly intertextual reading in Micah 4 and 7, especially with Isaiah, Jeremiah, Deuteronomy, Exodus, and the gospels; the dossier records only the parallels explained in the notes.
Historical dates appear approximately and sometimes debated in the notes; one should not treat internal chronologies as if they were independent proof.
Tyndale notes explain abundantly images and context in Micah 1, 4 and 7, but the coverage is selective and does not comment on all the details of each chapter.

The statements about future restoration, nations that pilgrim Zion and the ruler of Bethlehem are theological and interpretative in the notes; this dossier classifies them according to the source, without additional harmonizations.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the notes provided and therefore reflects the selective coverage of these sources. There is strong attention to Micah 1, 4 and 7, in addition to general mentions of the book structure and some historical data of 2 Kings and Jeremiah; other academic passages and debates not explained in the notes were left out. Where the source suggests possible alternative readings, such as the question of post-exile edition or the meaning of "spices in plowshares," this was maintained as debate/interpretation, without extrapolating. The distinction between the historical setting of the prophet and the possible final composition of the book was also preserved. No etymologies, exact chronologies or historical reconstructions that were not clearly present in the notes were introduced.
